pending_articles.title: Distinct input-output relationships between basal forebrain subnuclei underlie heterogeneous cholinergic modulation of the mouse cortex
pending_articles.content: The basal forebrain (BF) supports many behavioral functions via its brain-wide projections, which can be recruited independently and task specifically. However, the anatomical underpinnings for this functional heterogeneity are poorly understood. Here, we compared two mouse BF subnuclei, the horizontal diagonal band (HDB) and the substantial innominata (SI), in terms of their anatomical connectivity and functional recruitment. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we show that they target largely segregated forebrain regions, but their input comes from a partially overlapping subset of regions. However, many neurons within each region project to just one of the subnuclei, suggesting they can be recruited independently. To test this, we combined optogenetics and widefield Ca2+ imaging and showed that stimulating prefrontal cortical projections to the HDB or SI results in distinct large-scale patterns of cortical activity via a cholinergic mechanism. Our results provide an anatomical basis for the flexible, area-specific cholinergic modulation of brain function.
pending_articles.author: Pinto, L., Tan, J., Harter, A. M., Kolb, M., Lu, R.

pending_articles.title: Striatal dopamine availability peaks in adulthood and undergoes age-dependent modulation
pending_articles.content: Age is a risk factor for several psychiatric disorders. An adolescent peak in striatal dopamine availability is thought to contribute to the neuropsychiatric vulnerability. However, the lifespan trajectory of striatal dopamine release capacity is undefined in most species. Here, we measured lifespan trajectories of striatal dopamine in primates and rodents and identified a delayed developmental peak in adulthood and age-dependent changes in dopamine release regulation by GABA and acetylcholine across species.

pending_articles.title: Advanced meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control linked to absorptive depth
pending_articles.content: Advanced meditation can shift conscious experience from ordinary body- and world-centered awareness toward absorption, detachment and dissociation-like states, yet the neural mechanisms that stabilize these immersive states remain unclear. We studied 18 long-term meditators during eyes-open rest and Rajyoga meditation, a practice in which practitioners reduce bodily identification while enhancing inner self-awareness. We combined multidimensional neural approach including frontal EEG spectral power, temporal non-stationarity and corticothalamic neural-field modeling, because these measures probe underlying complementary levels of the brain state transition: the strength of neural activity, its temporal stability, and the circuit level inhibition-excitation gain mechanisms. This framework is especially relevant to meditation because oscillatory, temporal organization may distinguish stable meditative states, and corticothalamic dynamics are closely linked to arousal and conscious state regulation. We correlated meditation induced neural changes with subjective ratings of absorption and dissociation. Compared with rest, meditation was associated with higher beta1, beta2 and gamma power, with no change in the slower bands (delta, theta and alpha), and with lower beta-band temporal non-stationarity, indicating a more stable expression of fast cortical dynamics. Fitting the corticothalamic model to the EEG spectra showed stronger cortical inhibitory gain and lower effective intracortical gain, placing meditation in an inhibition-dominant regime, with lower gain in the loop between excitatory and inhibitory neurons within the cortex. During meditation, these model estimates were related to subjective absorption and showed trend level links with dissociation. Together, these findings suggest that Rajyoga meditation stabilizes cortical dynamics through inhibitory gain control, linking absorption (deep and steady attention on the meditation) to dissociation-like self-detachment.

pending_articles.title: Learned associations constrain anticipatory visual dynamics and enhance sensory and motor readiness to facilitate perceptual decisions
pending_articles.content: Learned cue target associations can guide attention to facilitate perceptual decision making, yet how they shape the content and dynamics of neural activity, and whether this facilitation reflects anticipatory preparation, post-target sensory enhancement, or both, remains unclear. Here, we used magnetoencephalography while participants made living/nonliving judgments about visual objects (e.g., cat/violin) with left- or right-hand button presses. Cue category associations were established through repeated pairings: predictive cues always preceded one target category, whereas uninformative cues preceded both categories equally often. Predictive cues facilitated behavioral responses despite limited explicit awareness of the learned associations. Representational similarity analysis showed that prediction preactivated target-specific representations in the visual cortex resembling target evoked activity before target onset. Prediction also elicited anticipatory, response specific motor beta suppression. Together, these findings supported anticipatory preparation, with little evidence of enhanced posttarget visual specificity. Posttarget visual specificity and anticipatory motor preparation independently predicted response speed, with hierarchical drift diffusion modeling linking greater visual specificity to faster evidence accumulation and stronger motor preparation to shorter nondecision time (a model parameter reflecting sensory encoding and motor execution). Beyond representational content, prediction also constrained the evolution of anticipatory visual population activity, and more constrained, stable early visual trajectories predicted faster responses. These population dynamics were associated with faster evidence accumulation, lower decision thresholds, and shorter non-decision time. Together, these findings suggest that associative memory facilitates perceptual decisions by shaping the content and dynamics of anticipatory neural activity, with partially dissociable contributions from visual processing and motor preparation.

pending_articles.title: Tri-Modal Single-Cell Atlas of Developing Human Brain
pending_articles.content: Epigenetic modifications, such as DNA methylation, evolve throughout development and aging, providing remarkable regulatory diversity and contributing to disease etiology, including neuropsychiatric disorders. However, how these regulatory layers interact across human brain development remains unclear. Leveraging ME-seq, we simultaneously mapped gene expression, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation in over 340,000 single nuclei from 40 human brain specimens spanning fetal development to adolescence. Chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation captured partially overlapping cis-regulatory associations. Developmental trajectories revealed distinct temporal kinetics: DNA methylation continued remodeling beyond major transcriptional and accessibility transitions, while developmental clocks yielded modality-dependent age estimates. Modality-specific regulatory networks converged on developmental transcription factors, whereas methylation-defined regulatory regions provided complementary annotations of neuropsychiatric genetic risk. Together, these findings establish DNA methylation as a persistent and complementary dimension of developmental regulation, linking prolonged remodeling to human brain maturation and disease susceptibility.

pending_articles.title: Hyperglycemia-responsive circRNA drives diabetic neuropathic pain by competing for PUM2 binding and promoting proNT3/CCL2 in DRG neurons
pending_articles.content: Diabetic neuropathic pain (DNP), one of the most common and debilitating complications of diabetes mellitus (DM), remains poorly managed by conventional analgesics, highlighting the urgent need to explore its etiology-associated mechanisms. Here, we identified a novel conserved circular RNA, cRps6kb1, that is significantly upregulated in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons across multiple mouse models of type 1 DM and type 2 DM, as well as in human donors with DNP. Blocking cRps6kb1 upregulation attenuated the increases in DRG neurotrophin-3 mRNA (Nt3), its encoded proneurotrophin-3 (proNT3), and downstream C-C chemokine ligand 2 (CCL2) expression, as well as the persistence of nociceptive hypersensitivity under the conditions of streptozotocin-induced type 1 DM or high-fat diet-fed type 2 DM. Conversely, mimicking cRps6kb1 upregulation increased DRG Nt3, proNT3, and CCL2 levels and produced DNP-like symptoms in naive mice. In addition, high glucose increased the expression of cRps6kb1 and Nt3 in cultured DRG neurons from mice and human donors. Mechanistically, upregulated cRps6kb1 competed with the Nt3 3'-untranslated region (3-UTR) for the translational repressor PUM2 binding, releasing PUM2 from the Nt3 3-UTR and enhancing Nt3 mRNA translation and stability. Thus, cRps6kb1 is a key contributor to DNP and represents a promising therapeutic target for its treatment.

pending_articles.title: A novel behavioral paradigm for characterizing anticipatory postural adjustments in mice
pending_articles.content: Voluntary movements perturb the body's equilibrium, and the nervous system limits this disturbance by generating anticipatory postural adjustments (APAs) that redistribute body weight before and during movement. APAs have been characterized extensively in humans and larger animal models, but the absence of a tractable behavioral assay in mice has limited access to the genetic and circuit-level tools needed to investigate their neural basis. Here, we describe a force-plate behavioral paradigm in which freely moving mice stand on four independent load cells, receive an auditory GO cue and initiate locomotion voluntarily without task-specific training. Using force recordings, high-speed video and markerless pose estimation, we show that mice initiate a step with a stereotyped sequence of weight shifts: the center of pressure (CoP) moves anteriorly and then laterally away from the swing side, the swing forepaw and diagonally opposite hindpaw unload, and body weight is carried by the remaining diagonal pair. A single principal component explained approximately 80% of the variance in the average trial, compared with approximately 50% when paw identity was shuffled. Pressure recordings identified rapid swing-forepaw unloading beginning, on average, 87.9 ms before lift-off. Head and ear movement began approximately 200 ms before lift-off, and an operational multimodal estimate placed the interval between the earliest detected postural movement and the onset of forepaw rotation at approximately 160-180 ms. Neuropixels recordings from the pontine reticular nucleus (PRN) and supplementary motor area (SMA), monosynaptic tracing of inputs to reticulospinal PRN neurons, and preliminary cell-ablation experiments identify the PRN as a candidate node in the circuitry supporting anticipatory postural control. This paradigm provides a platform for circuit-level investigation of postural control and its disruption in disease.

recently_processed.title: Transcriptional and DNA Methylation Changes in the Hippocampus and Prefrontal Cortex after Fractionated Cranial Radiation in Mice
recently_processed.content: Fractionated whole-brain irradiation is essential for treating brain tumors, but many long-term survivors develop cognitive decline whose molecular basis is poorly understood. We asked which cell types and gene programs change late after irradiation, how the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex compare, and whether DNA methylation changes affect the same genes or programs. Male and female mice received whole-brain irradiation (5 x 4 Gy) or anesthesia alone. Irradiated mice showed persistent deficits in executive function and spatial memory. Eleven weeks after irradiation, single-nucleus RNA sequencing and whole-genome bisulfite sequencing of pooled hippocampal (CA1-3) and prefrontal tissue showed cell-type-specific transcriptional changes in neurons of both regions. Both regions showed reduced ribosomal-protein gene expression and changes in adhesion genes, with reduced respiratory-chain genes in prefrontal neurons and bidirectional synaptic gene changes in hippocampus. Differentially methylated regions were enriched at promoters, with hypermethylation predominating in three of the four sex-by-region contrasts. Methylation and gene expression changes pointed to overlapping synaptic and signaling programs, largely through different genes.

recently_processed.title: A common neural axis links image distinctiveness and memorability
recently_processed.content: Stimulus-specific memorability, the tendency for people to remember and forget the same stimuli, is a powerful predictor of memory performance that is independent of the study and retrieval factors that have dominated memory research. Critically, memorability can be defined in two ways: "Hit-ability" (H-ability) and "false alarm-ability" (FA-ability), the probability of correctly recognizing studied items or falsely recognizing unstudied items, respectively. Although past work has suggested that these are dissociable facets of memorability, challenging single-factor explanations, we present neural and computational evidence that they share a common neural axis. The neural signature of high H-ability matched the signature for low FA-ability, showing that these parameters have inverse relationships with a common factor. Moreover, we show that image distinctiveness predicts the flipped relationship between H-ability and FA-ability in both behavior and neural activity, providing a unifying explanation of stimulus-specific memorability.

recently_processed.title: Neuropathological assessment of cerebrovascular integrity in Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy
recently_processed.content: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy neuropathological change (CTE-NC) is defined by perivascular deposits of phosphorylated tau, with lesions preferentially located at sulcal depths. We investigated whether CTE-NC is associated with structural changes to perivascular spaces (PVSs) or microvascular degeneration. Post-mortem middle frontal gyrus tissue from 11 CTE-NC cases and 11 age-matched controls was examined using immunohistochemistry. All CTE-NC cases exhibited pathognomonic lesions in this region. We quantified PVS width along with vessel lumen and PVS area, string vessel burden, pericyte density, and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarisation to the astrocytic endfoot. Total PVS width did not differ significantly between the groups in grey matter (P = 0.543) nor white matter (P = 0.468). Neither PVS area (sulcal depth, P = 0.097; gyral crest, P = 0.645) nor PVS-to-lumen area ratio (sulcal depth, P = 0.454; gyral crest, P = 0.307) differed significantly. Similarly, there were no significant differences in total microvascular length (p = 0.693), string vessel burden (p = 0.128), pericyte density (p = 0.589), or AQP4 endfoot enrichment (p = 0.538). We therefore found no evidence of large-scale PVS enlargement, lumen narrowing, capillary degeneration, pericyte loss, or altered AQP4 endfoot enrichment in CTE-NC at the locations and spatial scales investigated. Taken together, these findings suggest that the pathognomonic perivascular tau lesion is not associated with a classical small vessel degenerative phenotype in CTE-NC. However, that does not exclude more subtle molecular, functional, or ultrastructural changes at the interface between vessels, the perivascular space, and surrounding brain tissue.
